A student in a Form 5 class dissolves salt in water until no more will dissolve at a fixed temperature. The solution obtained is called a saturated solution.

Which statement gives the correct meaning of the solubility of a salt?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Solubility is always quoted for a stated temperature, for a fixed mass of solvent (100 g of water), and for a saturated solution, that is, the maximum amount that can dissolve.

### Solution

Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of water at a given temperature to form a saturated solution.

- The statement using 100 g of solution mixes up solution and solvent.
- The statement about the solute dissolved when the solution is first stirred ignores that solubility is a maximum, reached only at saturation.
- The statement using 1 dm$^3$ of water at any temperature ignores the standard 100 g of water and the fixed temperature.

choix.texte: The mass of solute that dissolves in 1 dm$^3$ of water at any temperature.
The mass of solute present in 100 g of any solution.
The mass of solute that has dissolved in water when the solution is first stirred.
The maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of water at a given temperature.

The table gives the solubility of two salts, X and Y, in g per 100 g of water.

| Temperature / $^\circ$C | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Salt X (g per 100 g of water) | 13 | 32 | 64 | 110 | 169 |
| Salt Y (g per 100 g of water) | 36 | 36 | 37 | 38 | 40 |

What mass of salt X is needed to make a saturated solution at 40 $^\circ$C in 200 g of water?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The tabulated solubility is for 100 g of water. For another mass of water, scale the solubility in proportion: $\text{mass of solute} = \text{solubility} \times \frac{\text{mass of water}}{100}$.

### Solution

At 40 $^\circ$C the solubility of X is 64 g per 100 g of water.

$$\text{mass of X} = 64 \times \frac{200}{100} = 128 \text{ g}$$

- 64 g forgets to double for 200 g of water.
- 32 g reads the 20 $^\circ$C column.
- 256 g doubles the value twice.

A saturated solution of salt X containing 100 g of water at 60 $^\circ$C is cooled to 20 $^\circ$C. What mass of crystals of X forms?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On cooling a saturated solution, the mass of crystals formed equals the difference between the solubilities at the two temperatures (for the same 100 g of water).

### Solution

Solubility of X at 60 $^\circ$C = 110 g per 100 g of water; at 20 $^\circ$C = 32 g per 100 g of water.

Mass of crystals $= 110 - 32 = 78$ g.

- 110 g is the mass dissolved at 60 $^\circ$C, not the mass that crystallises.
- 32 g is the mass still dissolved at 20 $^\circ$C.
- 142 g wrongly adds the two solubilities.

A student adds 40 g of salt X to 50 g of water at 40 $^\circ$C and stirs thoroughly.

Which statement describes the mixture correctly?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Find how much solute the given mass of water can hold at that temperature (scale the tabulated solubility), then compare it with the mass added. If more is added than can dissolve, the solution is saturated and the excess stays undissolved.

### Solution

At 40 $^\circ$C, 100 g of water dissolves 64 g of X, so 50 g of water dissolves $64 \times \frac{50}{100} = 32$ g.

40 g is more than 32 g, so only 32 g dissolves. The solution is saturated and $40 - 32 = 8$ g of X remains undissolved.

- "Unsaturated, all dissolved" would need the water to hold at least 40 g.
- 24 g undissolved comes from using the 20 $^\circ$C solubility (16 g in 50 g of water).
- A supersaturated solution cannot form simply by stirring at constant temperature.

choix.texte: The solution is unsaturated and all 40 g of X dissolves.
The solution is saturated and 8 g of X remains undissolved.
The solution is saturated and 24 g of X remains undissolved.
The solution is supersaturated and all 40 g of X dissolves.

Two saturated solutions, each containing 250 g of water, are prepared at 80 $^\circ$C, one with salt X and one with salt Y. Each is cooled to 20 $^\circ$C.

(a) Calculate the mass of crystals formed from each solution.

(b) Explain why cooling is a good way to obtain crystals of X but not of Y.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For each salt, crystals formed $=$ (solubility at the higher temperature $-$ solubility at the lower temperature) $\times \frac{\text{mass of water}}{100}$.

### Solution

(a) Salt X: $(169 - 32) \times \frac{250}{100} = 137 \times 2.5 = 342.5$ g.

Salt Y: $(40 - 36) \times \frac{250}{100} = 4 \times 2.5 = 10$ g.

(b) The solubility of X changes a great deal with temperature (169 g to 32 g per 100 g of water), so a large mass crystallises on cooling. The solubility of Y hardly changes with temperature (40 g to 36 g), so only a very small mass of crystals forms and cooling is not effective.

A saturated solution of salt X with a total mass of 420 g is prepared at 60 $^\circ$C. It is cooled to 20 $^\circ$C. Then 50 g of water is allowed to evaporate from the solution at 20 $^\circ$C.

Calculate the total mass of crystals of X that have formed at the end.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A saturated solution at a given temperature contains 100 g of water for every (100 + solubility) g of solution. First find the masses of water and salt in the solution, then find how much salt the remaining water can still hold at each new stage.

### Solution

At 60 $^\circ$C: 100 g of water + 110 g of X = 210 g of saturated solution. So 420 g of solution (twice as much) contains 200 g of water and 220 g of X.

After cooling to 20 $^\circ$C: 200 g of water can hold only $32 \times 2 = 64$ g of X. Crystals formed $= 220 - 64 = 156$ g.

After evaporating 50 g of water: 150 g of water can hold $32 \times 1.5 = 48$ g of X. The extra crystals are $64 - 48 = 16$ g.

Total crystals $= 156 + 16 = 172$ g.
